# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Old Model of Toughness

When college students described toughness, words like "hard-nosed," "gritty," "playing through pain," and "stoic" came to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, "perseverance" ranked highest. The traditional image: a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back in place, or Craig MacTavish (last NHL player without a helmet). This view equates toughness with overcoming obstacles through perseverance, discipline, and stoicism.

Bobby Knight exemplifies this old model. He won over 900 games, three NCAA championships, and a perfect 1976 season. He defined toughness as "being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself." But his methods included: hanging tampons from lockers of players he thought "soft"; a 1991 tirade ("This is absolute fucking bullshit... I will fucking run your ass right into the ground"); bringing toilet paper with shit to show players what he thought of them; and choking a player on video. All in the name of toughness founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear.

## Tough Parenting

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind classified parenting styles by two factors: responsiveness (attunement to children's needs) and demandingness (expectations and control). Authoritarian parents are high in demandingness, low in responsiveness—relying on fear, threats, punishment, and "because I said so." In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally." Another study found 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft on children. The "just right" Goldilocks fit is high demand with high support.

## To Be Callous

The language of toughness reveals callousness: teams called "soft," needing "hardening up," told to "show no signs of weakness." We romanticize the Karate Kid narrative. In youth sports, children are made to run laps or do burpees not for training adaptation but to "toughen them up." In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found frequent vomiting after workouts; parents justified it as "necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior." We tell children to "man up" or "stop being a pussy." As *A League of Their Own* summarized: "There’s no crying in baseball!" Toughness is tied to masculinity and machismo—images of The Rock or Vin Diesel, not small females. Yet women consistently handle pain better than men.

## Consequences of the Callous View

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair, 19, showed profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints. Coaches yelled "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." After the final sprint, it took trainers 34 minutes to take him off the field and another 28 minutes to call 911—1 hour 28 minutes total. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke.

Rhabdomyolysis, once rare, now occurs frequently from extreme workouts designed not to improve fitness but to "test" athletes. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, these workouts aim to "toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots."

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, higher substance abuse. In sport, it's linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those raised in authoritarian environments coped worse with military challenges. One young athlete explained: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger... I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished." Motivation becomes avoidance of punishment, not internal drive.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. Real toughness is "experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It's navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can."

Pete Carroll, who lost his NFL job in the 1990s then won both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl, builds toughness through inner drive, embracing challenges, and bouncing back. He said: "Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do." Other successful coaches using humanistic approaches: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D'Antoni (who told Magness, "We keep it positive here"). As Ken Reed summarized: "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach."

A 2008 Eastern Washington study of nearly 200 basketball players concluded that promoting mental toughness "does not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach’s ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

## A Personal Journey

Magness recounts racing the Don Bowden Mile at Cal. At 900 meters into the 1,609-meter race, he experienced a strange high-pitched gasp, then couldn't breathe. He collapsed. After a year of tests (scopes, echocardiograms, treadmill tests), allergist Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—vocal cords shut on inhalation instead of opening. Triggers include "strong emotions" and stress. Magness's old strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. He had to learn to relax and keep steady at the moment of peak discomfort.

The four pillars of real toughness:
- **Pillar 1:** Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
- **Pillar 2:** Listen to Your Body
- **Pillar 3:** Respond Instead of React
- **Pillar 4:** Transcend Discomfort

As podcaster Rich Roll told Magness: "Everybody goes through shit in their life. Nobody escapes obstacles." Real toughness isn't about bulldozing through; it's about navigating discomfort to make the best decision possible.
